items.question: What do you think has driven improvements in AI model costs and latency?
items.object: Improvements in AI model costs and latency
items.answer: Part of it is, I think, better architecture. It's kind of crazy how good the models are at acting like humans. We've just been seeing an explosion of techniques there.
quotes: Part of it is, I think, better architecture. It's kind of crazy how good the models are at acting like humans. We've just been seeing an explosion of techniques there.

items.question: How do you see competition with Nvidia in AI chips developing over the next couple of years?
items.object: Competition with Nvidia in AI chips
items.answer: Yeah, I spend a fair amount of time thinking about the chips. I think certainly there are lots of competitors trying to enter this space. AMD has been here for a while. Obviously Nvidia is dominant for a couple reasons: they design very good chips and build very good software, and that creates this ecosystem where people build software on top of that. But I think certainly we'll see a lot of competitors entering the space. As the workload starts to coalesce around the architecture side, you know, transformer and so on, it becomes a little bit easier to design chips for that kind of workload. If you just focus on inference, I think AMD has certain advantages. They have larger memory and so on, so we're starting to see folks picking that up. On the training side, it's a little bit more difficult. Networking is one of the main bottlenecks, and NVIDIA is certainly ahead there. But I think people understand the challenges to build good training chips and good inference chips. It comes down to execution. This space is really exciting. I talk to lots of folks who are designing new chips, either inference or training. I would expect in the next couple years maybe some of the workload will become multi-silicon. They'll probably run on different chips rather than, right now, I'd say 90% on Nvidia.

items.question: How stable do you think AI model architectures are as a basis for designing chips?
items.object: AI model architecture stability for chip design
items.answer: I think on the architecture side, from a very high level, it looks like it is sort of stabilized around transformer. But once you look a little bit closer, there's actually quite a bit of change around that. The most recent one in the last couple years has been mixture of experts, where you make the model much, much larger, more parameters, but sparser. That has certain trade-offs: you need more memory, but maybe the amount of compute you do is a little bit smaller. Even that presents difficulty for some chipmakers, because maybe they were designing for a dense model where it's very uniform compute, and now you have something sparse, so it's a little bit harder to design for. Or some of the stuff changing around attention, which has been around since 2017.

items.question: Why do you see changes to attention architectures as a challenge for AI chip design?
items.object: Attention architecture changes and AI chip design
items.answer: I think there are changes here and there that make some of this stuff difficult. DeepSeek has this thing, multi-head latent attention, that looks a little bit different than attention. For example, they have very large head dimension, and if your systolic matrix multiplication engine has a certain size, maybe it doesn't fit. Weird things like that once you look underneath the cover.

items.question: How do you think evolving coding and agent workloads change the challenge of designing AI chips?
items.object: AI chip design for evolving coding and agent workloads
items.answer: There are new workloads, like coding workloads like Cursor and Windsurf and so on. There's a kind of agent workload where it's not so much just running the model, but also making tool calls, running a Python interpreter, doing web search, and so on. That presents challenges for how you design the chip. If the chip is very much focused on just running the model as fast as possible, you might neglect things like how you're going to connect to the host to run a web search. Even though from a high level the architecture has kind of stabilized, underneath the cover there's still a lot going on, and part of it is the workload is also changing. I think it's a constant race of how fast can you execute and adapt to these new workloads.

items.question: Why do you expect AI inference workloads to diversify beyond NVIDIA chips?
items.object: Diversification of AI inference hardware beyond NVIDIA
items.answer: On the inference side, some of it will diversify. We're starting to see companies like Cerebras and Groq and SambaNova really presenting a serious challenge. They were pitching, hey, we can get very, very low-latency inference, and that's fantastic for some use cases. We talk to customers who really care about as low latency as possible and are willing to pay more for that. We're starting to see more of these niche areas where people really care about low latency, or some people really care about very large batch, high-throughput inference. Those things are massive data processing or synthetic data generation or RL training, where you have to roll out and generate as many trajectories as possible. I would say it's going to diversify simply because the workloads are going to diversify, whether low latency or high throughput or something else. Maybe video generation will require a different profile in terms of how much compute and memory you need.

items.question: How do you think an AI chip startup should approach betting on future workloads?
items.object: AI chip startups’ bets on future workloads
items.answer: If you're a startup, you have to make a bet. You invest, and you have to make an outsized bet. You could bet that maybe chatbots will go away and the thing that people really care about is video generation models or world models or robotics or something. You make that bet and say, okay, that's probably going to be 50% of the workload. How would we design for that workload? And you hope that your bet will be correct. That's the role of a startup. If you don't place a bet and say, "I'm just going to optimize for the general workload," then the incumbents are going to just out-execute you.

items.question: How do you decide which chip ecosystems to spend your time working in?
items.object: Choosing which chip ecosystems to work in
items.answer: I personally work with lots of folks from Nvidia, AMD, Google, Amazon, and so on. I spend a lot of my time on Nvidia chips simply because this is what we have right now. That's what most people use. I think they design very good chips and very good software for that, so that allows me to do interesting things. That's kind of what I'm after: can you do interesting things? We've worked with the folks at AMD; for example, they had a version of FlashAttention, and we worked with them to integrate that in the public repo.

items.question: What role do you see abstractions playing in scaling optimization work across GPUs and other accelerators?
items.object: Abstractions for GPU and accelerator optimization
items.answer: Nowadays I'm thinking a lot more about what abstractions we need, not just for Nvidia chips but for GPUs and accelerators in general. I spend time at the lowest level trying to get the maximum performance out of these chips. But as we scale at Together, we think about how to get other people we hire productive, and part of it is building abstractions that will work on Nvidia chips and potentially other chips as well. The other thing I'm excited about is what kind of abstractions we build so AI can do some of this work for us. The answer isn't quite clear yet, but as technical leaders it's about building the right abstraction so other people can get onboarded quickly, so the things you do could work across different kinds of chips or workloads.

items.question: How do you assess Triton as an abstraction for working across different GPU chips?
items.object: Triton and the trade-off between cross-chip abstractions and performance
items.answer: I think we have some. This is a usual trade-off. Triton is really good, and it supports Nvidia chips, AMD GPUs, Intel GPUs, and so on. That requires them to design a front end and then there's a back end, and different companies will contribute code to the back end. Triton is quite good, and a lot of companies are betting on that. Meta, for example, PyTorch compile will generate Triton code and rely on Triton to generate code for Nvidia or AMD. But that's the usual trade-off: if you don't control at the lowest level, maybe you give up some performance. It's about where that trade-off point is. If you give up 5% performance and become 3x more productive, that's an acceptable trade-off. But if you give up too much performance, maybe people would go with something a little more—

items.question: How do you think about hardware portability as GPU architectures evolve?
items.object: Hardware portability across GPU generations
items.answer: Designing for humans is really, really hard. I would say hardware portability is kind of a myth. Even for Nvidia chips, generation to generation they change a lot, and I think that's kind of the only way we get more performance out of these chips. It's not like a CPU where year to year maybe you get 5% to 10% faster and your old code just works. Even for Nvidia, every generation they essentially have to rewrite all the code, because the way to get more FLOPs is to build more specialized components, maybe lower precision, maybe a different way to synchronize between different parts of the chips. Nvidia also essentially rewrites their software every two years or so. Even portability between generations isn't quite there, so those abstractions would be valuable even just to help you with each subsequent generation of chips from the same manufacturer.

items.question: How do you evaluate the GPU programming abstractions in Triton and Modular’s Mojo?
items.object: GPU programming abstractions in Triton and Modular’s Mojo
items.answer: I think Triton has very compelling abstractions. They even have something a little lower level, Gluon, where it exposes more of the hardware at the cost of maybe being less general. The folks at Modular have been building this language, Mojo. I think it's super cool. They have some of the right abstractions. It's just about execution, because people are going to look at it and be like, okay, how fast are you on Nvidia chips? That's a really, in some sense unfair question, but that's what people care about. They would design the abstractions and then have to do custom work to make their code run really well on Nvidia chips, then do a little custom work for AMD chips. It's about how much you want to do the customization, trading off performance.

items.question: How do you interpret the proliferation of domain-specific languages for writing GPU kernels?
items.object: Domain-specific languages and abstractions for GPU kernel programming
items.answer: We're seeing more and more of these libraries or domain-specific languages. The folks at Stanford have ThunderKittens. There's TileLang. Google has Mosaic GPU. I'm sure I'm forgetting some. People realize there's a problem: we don't have the right abstractions yet. It's actually kind of painful to train new engineers to write very performant GPU kernels. The answer is to build abstractions. We're very much in the phase where we're iterating pretty quickly. That's why we see so many domain-specific languages coming out.

items.question: Where do you expect better abstractions for high-performance GPU programming to come from?
items.object: Abstractions for high-performance GPU programming
items.answer: People approach this from two angles. One is from the machine learning side. They think about what kind of workload we have and what primitives are necessary to express those workloads. A lot of workloads, let's say inference, are very much about how can I move memory as fast as possible. Inference is usually memory-bound. Or how do I do matrix multiply as fast as possible, and what are the primitives I want to express there? The other angle is people thinking from the hardware side. They have really cool specialized components on the chips, and they're thinking about abstractions on how to expose these. One thing Nvidia has been really good at is designing chips that are more asynchronous, because matrix multiplication is getting so fast. It's ridiculous that everything else becomes much slower. It becomes much more important to overlap the computation of matrix multiplication and everything else. How do you design abstractions that allow this asynchronous execution? Things like pipelines and synchronizations. I'd say that's where the abstractions are going to come from, either from the workload side or from the hardware side. I think it will become clearer in maybe one or two years.

items.answer: I think models are starting to become useful for this stuff, actually very recently. This really surprised me. On one level, what people are after is fully automatic GPU kernel writing: you describe the problem and the LM will generate the kernel for you. Maybe we're there with some other areas, like simple Python scripts, data analysis, or web front ends. Could we do that for GPU kernels?

items.question: How do you assess the prospects for language models that automatically write GPU kernels?
items.object: Fully automatic GPU kernel writing with language models
items.answer: I think we're very, very early. These models can generate some simple kernels, like element-wise: you take in an array and do some operation on each element, or do some kind of reduction like summing and some normalization things like that. The models can do a reasonably good job. But once it gets a little more complicated, these models just don't generate correct code. I think it's a function of not having enough training data. Training data is really tough for this stuff, because if you scrape the internet for kernel code, you'll get class projects and documentation meant for GPUs maybe three generations ago, things you shouldn't be doing now. Training data is really difficult. The answer is probably to start with some expert-level data and then generate synthetic data out of that, or hook up to a tool like a compiler and profiler so you can get lots of training data, or get the right environment. I think it will be solved in a year or two, but it's certainly a difficult problem.

items.question: How do you see the path to making AI models useful for GPU kernel generation?
items.object: AI models for GPU kernel generation
items.answer: I don't think this kind of data is private. There are a couple of places where you have expert-level code, but I think it's more about the workflow: how do you start from a small amount of expert-level data and generate lots of synthetic data? The folks at GPU Mode have been really trying to do this. They took the PyTorch compiler, which generates code to go from PyTorch to Triton, this lower-level kernel code, and they could generate, I think, 15,000 pairs of these programs. You have to be a little creative. There's just not that much data on the internet, so you have to be creative about how you're going to generate this kind of data. That's one angle if you want fully automatic kernel generation. We're super early there. The other side is: can models work alongside humans? I've been pleasantly surprised that these models are actually quite useful.

items.question: How do you explain the decline in LLM inference costs since ChatGPT debuted?
items.object: The decline in LLM inference costs since ChatGPT debuted
items.answer: On one side, on the modeling side, people have just trained much better models for the same number of parameters. Part of it is much more data; part of it is, I think, better architecture. That certainly helps. People invent new sorts of efficient attention and so on. That's on the modeling side: models getting much better for the same number of parameters. The other side is inference optimization, and we've been seeing an explosion of techniques there. In the early days, as a whole, we didn't understand the bottlenecks of inference. After a while, people realized it's a lot about data movement: moving the weights in and out of memory, moving the KV cache, which is the part of the attention operation where you need to store the entire history to make the next prediction. A lot of optimizations are around how do we reduce the data movement. You could quantize the model. Instead of typically using 16 bits per parameter, now eight bits is pretty common and some new models are using four bits. There's some work using one or two bits, which is pretty crazy. You see this compelling trade-off: as you quantize the model, a lot of times you pretty much don't lose any quality, and that requires fairly sophisticated techniques, but it has worked amazingly well. The most recent OpenAI release, GPT-OSS, has most of the layers in four bits, which is crazy. They have, I think, 120 billion parameters, but because each is using four bits, you could fit that in 60 gigabytes or something, and that has translated to really good inference performance.

items.question: How do you think co-designing model architecture and hardware helps make inference more efficient?
items.object: Co-design of model architecture and hardware for efficient inference
items.answer: As people understand much better, people on both sides are talking to each other a lot more. I think FlashAttention was kind of like that: there were people who understood the hardware really well and people who understood the algorithm and model really well. As you combine these ideas, you see exactly what the bottleneck on the hardware side is. How do I change the algorithm? For FlashAttention, we realized memory access was the main bottleneck, and we figured out a new way to rewrite the attention algorithm to reduce memory access. We're seeing that a lot for inference. An example is this variant of attention from DeepSeek called multi-head latent attention, where they realized a lot of time is spent moving the KV cache, which is a summary of the history. They realized they could make the KV cache much smaller with a latent projection, projecting on a much smaller space. That works really well in DeepSeek. In the paper, they said they were able to serve this model very efficiently. Another example is mixture of experts, where for each query, for each token, you don't use all the parameters in the model. There's some sparsity, so you use some part of the model. In the last couple years, the trend has been making the model sparser and sparser.

items.question: How do you understand the role of increasing model sparsity in recent inference improvements?
items.object: Increasing model sparsity and inference efficiency
items.answer: The first open-source model from Mistral was maybe a year or two ago. They activated two experts out of eight per layer, a ratio of 25%. But now for DeepSeek and the OpenAI model, you activate, I think, four out of 128 for GPT-OSS, or something. That's a factor of 32, and we're getting sparser and sparser. That's really good if you serve lots and lots of users. People are really understanding the workload. They're co-designing the architecture with inference, and I would say that's where a lot of the improvement has come from: this co-design between model and the inference stack.

items.question: How do you see the remaining potential for hardware improvements to speed up AI inference?
items.object: Hardware improvements for AI inference
items.answer: I think as a whole we've picked off a lot of low-hanging fruit, for sure, but I think there's still lots to do. One is on the hardware side. For a while, because you couldn't really predict what the workload is going to be two years from now, you couldn't specialize very well. But as the architecture has gotten a little more stable, people designing chips are optimizing for inference now. Low precision gets really good native hardware support; all the networking gets really good, because as the model gets larger, with things like mixture of experts, models get larger but you don't activate all the parameters. You might need multiple GPUs or chips to store the model, and networking becomes much more important. On the hardware side it would probably be 2x or 3x just in one year.

items.question: How do you see model architectures like Mamba contributing to further gains in inference speed?
items.object: Mamba and model architectures that compress inference history
items.answer: One is pushing on model architecture. I've worked on things like Mamba. Instead of storing the entire history as a KV cache, you could have the model compress that history into a smaller state vector. Of course that's going to have certain trade-offs, but we've seen pretty good success with this. I think this is going to be especially important for large-batch inference, which is what some workloads are demanding these days. With test-time compute and reasoning, you want the model to explore lots of trajectories or chains of thought at the same time. I think Google came up with Gemini Deep Think, which was the idea: they were winning IMO gold medals and so on by exploring multiple paths at the same time. That means you're doing model inference on hundreds of sequences at the same time, and there the KV cache becomes a much bigger problem. You could try to get the model to compress that KV cache. That was the direction we were going with Mamba, and there have been a bunch of other variants along that idea. On the model side it's going to be 2x or 3x.

items.question: How do you think about the priorities of using AI models to generate synthetic training data?
items.object: Large-batch synthetic data generation and models' ability to imitate humans
items.answer: There is the very large batch: I don't care so much about latency, I just want as high throughput as possible. This is important for things like generating synthetic data. A lot of the way people are training models now is they have a small amount of expert-level data or human annotation data. Let's say you're an airline and you're trying to build an AI agent to resolve customer complaints or conflicts. They have a small amount of really good data, and then you can generate tons of synthetic data out of that. It's kind of crazy how good the models are at acting like humans. You can say, "Can you act as if you're this kind of customer from New York who's annoyed that their flight is delayed out of LaGuardia?" Models are surprisingly good at acting as humans. I'm scared that we've taught them the capabilities to be angry New Yorkers at an airport. That's not humanity at its finest.

items.question: How do you think running inference at scale helps you allocate compute between interactive queries and batch workloads?
items.object: Fleet-level optimization for inference workloads
items.answer: This is where maybe running at scale really helps. We call it fleet-level optimization, where if you're running inference on thousands of GPUs, you can dynamically change the cluster allocation. A simple example is running batch inference, batch API. OpenAI has an option for that; we also have an option. If we see that the cluster is not so busy with these more interactive queries, we can send in these batch queries that can soak up the compute. As a result, we provide, I think, 50% discount on batch API, and I think OpenAI does the same. DeepSeek probably does that too.

items.question: How do you see the remaining opportunities for inference optimization as open-source tools like vLLM and SGLang mature?
items.object: Opportunities for inference optimization as open-source tooling matures
items.answer: Early on there were lots of low-hanging fruits. If you write reasonable kernels, if you build a reasonable inference engine, you get much better results than what was out there. But now the open-source tooling is getting very good. Things like vLLM and SGLang are very popular and have gotten to production-level quality. We work with these folks and contribute. The baseline has gotten so much better. But there are also newer and newer use cases. Customers come to us and say, "We really care about prefix caching," or, "We really care about low latency because in our application we need this requirement." Or, "We're actually not doing text, we're doing video," and that's a different trade-off, much more throughput-oriented. We work with some of those customers. Even as the open-source tooling and libraries get so much better, the workloads are evolving so fast that there's always new stuff to do. There's an explosion of ways to extract value out of these models. That's why we see so many startups building on these models, and as a result the workload is going to evolve rapidly.

items.question: Where do you see the gap between what existing foundation models can offer robotics and what robots still need to learn?
items.object: Foundation models for robot control and the missing interaction data
items.answer: We can initialize a model controlling a robot with some of the foundation models that we already have. You can use a language model to do the planning. If you ask a robot to pick up a coffee cup, then the language model can say, go walk over to that table and pick up the coffee, and so on. What's missing, I think, is this kind of interacting and acting in the world, because we just don't have data for that. We have language data—

items.question: Why do you think robots need to process information at multiple resolutions and time scales?
items.object: Multi-resolution, multi-time-scale information processing in robots
items.answer: I think robots kind of have to process information in a multi-resolution, multi-time-scale way. If you're controlling the joints, you have to act very rapidly.
quotes: The other one is robots kind of have to process information in a multi-resolution, multi-time-scale way. If you're controlling the joints, you have to act very rapidly.

rubrics.text: The response states that controlling a robot’s joints requires acting on a rapid time scale.

items.question: How do you think a robot's AI architecture should account for tasks operating on different time scales?
items.object: Robot AI architectures that account for different time scales
items.answer: Taking time scale explicitly into account: do I want to do very lightweight computation to just control the joints, or do I want to do much heavier-weight reasoning to plan the optimal route for the robot? I think it's going to be this composite system initialized from language models, vision models, audio models, world models. How do you stitch them together? That's the big question.
quotes: Taking time scale explicitly into account: do I want to do very lightweight computation to just control the joints, or do I want to do much heavier-weight reasoning to plan the optimal route for the robot? I think it's going to be this composite system initialized from language models, vision models, audio models, world models. How do you stitch them together? That's the big question.

The response envisions a robot’s AI architecture as a composite of models from different modalities.
The response identifies how to integrate the component models as a central open question for a composite robot AI architecture.

items.question: Why do you prefer combining your work at Together with being a professor at Princeton?
items.object: Combining startup work at Together with a professorship at Princeton
items.answer: My answer is it's going to be personal. For every person it's going to be different. For me personally, I like being both in a startup and being a professor. They present different modes of thinking and execution. On the startup side it's very fun because we move fast. If there's things we want to do, we can get it done in days or weeks or at most months. That's the horizon that we plan for. It's very fun. You get a team of really good people, they can execute very fast and you accomplish great things. I'm very proud of the work the team has done at Together. On the academia side, it's a little bit longer time horizon, and the problems we think about are maybe more speculative. We don't solve the problem that needs a solution in a month. We think about, if the world is moving in that direction in two or three years, what are the interesting questions to ask and challenges to solve in one or two years? Working with students has been fun and rewarding because we get to think about questions that are intrinsically interesting. Obviously, there are trade-offs. The amount of compute in academia is much smaller. The way you evaluate it is: are your ideas interesting, rather than does it work and run really fast? That's a different set of evaluation. In academia you have more freedom to think deeply about longer-horizon problems. I happen to like both modes of operation, so that's why I'm still at Princeton as a professor and still involved in the startup.

items.question: How do you understand the respective roles of academia and industry in developing AI ideas?
items.object: The roles of academia and industry in developing AI ideas
items.answer: Ultimately I think it's maybe a mix of exploration and exploitation. At a macro level, academia's role is more on exploration. The funding usually comes from the government. The government cares about whether you can explore lots and lots of ideas to see maybe 5% or 10% work out. As an investor, as a VC, that's the mode you operate in as well: we're going to explore lots of ideas; maybe 5% or 10% become incredibly important. One example is attention. Even though it got famous with the Google paper, it actually came out of work at Mila with Dmitri and Yoshua Bengio and other folks. It was coming out of academia. If you think of the other components in the current architecture, the Adam optimizer was Jimmy Ba at Toronto and other folks. LayerNorm also, Jimmy. Lots of what we have now came out of academia because the role of academia is to explore lots and lots of ideas, and some will work. Then the role of big companies and startups is they take some of these ideas, innovate on them, execute really fast, and understand what the market needs, what product they should build. They have much bigger financial power to make some of these bigger ideas happen.

items.question: How do you make sense of investors funding AI research ventures that aren't planning to build products?
items.object: Venture funding for AI research ventures without near-term products
items.answer: It's kind of crazy the kind of funding folks are getting. Ilya SSI explicitly said, "We're not going to build any product." People want to give him money because he's Ilya, for sure. Some of the folks, like you said, in robotics are doing that. In AI, some of these risks are starting to pay off, so people on the investing side are much more willing to put in money.

items.question: Why do you expect open-source models to get closer in quality to closed-source models over the next year?
items.object: Open-source models’ quality relative to closed-source models over the next year
items.answer: I would say closer. I think the scaling now is more on the RL side, and that relies more on tooling than just raw compute. I think open source is going to do really well there.

items.question: What developments in AI do you think deserve more attention?
items.object: Data developments in AI, including synthetic data and model-based rephrasing
items.answer: Definitely data. I think data is always a little bit underhyped. A lot has happened on the data side. Synthetic data, using models to rephrase, has had a huge impact that maybe people have paid less attention to.

items.question: What do you think of the video generation applications Pika and Hedra have built using Together?
items.object: Pika and Hedra's video generation applications built on Together
items.answer: We worked with some of these video generation companies like Pika and Hedra, and they're generating viral TikTok videos with the models they train on Together and do inference on Together. It's been amazing.
